analysis.one_liner: Bans former members of Congress from lobbying for life and tightens revolving-door rules for staff and lobbyists.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan anti-revolving-door bill was referred to the Senate Homeland Security Committee in October 2019 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would turn the current two-year (Senate) and one-year (House) lobbying bans for former members of Congress into a lifetime ban, and stretch the cooling-off period for senior congressional staff from one year to six. It would also bar registered lobbyists and foreign agents from working in congressional offices they lobbied for six years, create a searchable public website (lobbyists.gov) listing ex-lawmakers hired by large lobbying firms, and raise the maximum civil penalty for lobbying disclosure violations from $200,000 to $500,000.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens, who would see fewer former lawmakers and senior staff move straight into lobbying jobs where they sell access to their ex-colleagues; and the public generally, through a searchable public database showing which lobbying firms employ former members of Congress.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a lifetime ban on former Senators, House Members, and elected congressional officers from lobbying Congress, replacing the current two-year (Senate) or one-year (House) cooling-off periods [S2][S3].
Extends the post-employment lobbying ban for congressional officers, personal, committee, and leadership staff from one year to six years [S2][S3].
Bars registered lobbyists and agents of foreign principals from being hired by a Member or committee they had substantial lobbying contact with, for six years [S3].

Requires large lobbying firms to file annual public lists of former members of Congress and highly paid former legislative officials they employ or pay as consultants, posted on a searchable government website, with filings sent to the U.S. Attorney for D.C. to check for underreporting [S3].
Raises the maximum civil penalty for lobbying disclosure violations from $200,000 to $500,000 [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Lobbying firms and their corporate clients, who would face steeper penalties and public disclosure of the ex-lawmakers on their payrolls; and former members of Congress and senior staff, who would lose a well-worn path to six-figure lobbying careers after leaving office.

drawbacks.text: A lifetime ban is broad: it applies to any lobbying contact with any congressional office, and critics of long cooling-off periods note it can push former members into unregistered 'strategic consulting' roles that fall outside lobbying disclosure rules entirely — the same firms could keep paying them without the work ever being labeled lobbying (general policy-mechanism knowledge; the bill's ban covers registered lobbying contacts, not consulting [S3]).
The bill itself includes an escape valve: the six-year ban on hiring lobbyists into congressional offices can be waived by the ethics committees 'based on a compelling national need' [S3].

The new public reporting requirement applies only to 'substantial lobbying entities' — firms with more than three registered lobbyists — so small firms and individual paid consultants to ex-lawmakers would not have to file [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core measures — a much longer revolving-door cooling-off period for members and staff, and public disclosure of which lobbying firms hire ex-lawmakers — are straightforwardly aimed at reducing the sale of congressional access, and the costs fall on lobbying firms and departing officials rather than on the public. The design has real gaps (a consulting loophole the ban does not reach, a waiver clause, a reporting threshold that exempts smaller shops), but these are limits on effectiveness, not costs borne by ordinary people. On balance a modest but genuine good-government reform.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Michael Bennet introduced the Close the Revolving Door Act of 2019 on October 17, 2019, joined by Sens. Cory Gardner and Jon Tester as cosponsors [S1][S3][S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs that same day [S5].
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — is recorded; the full action history ends with the referral [S5].
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill was never reintroduced or passed in that Congress [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lobbying firms, corporate interests that hire former members of Congress, and the departing lawmakers and senior staff who monetize their connections were all better off, because the bill never left committee and the revolving door stayed open.

for.name: Sen. Michael Bennet
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its sponsorship.

against.name: Sen. Ron Johnson
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after it was referred to his committee.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Held the Senate majority; the bill, though referred with a Republican cosponsor, never advanced to a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a bipartisan, if small, coalition at introduction — a Democratic sponsor with one Republican and one Democratic cosponsor — but the lack of committee action meant the partisan shape of any real fight never got recorded.

industries.note: The bill extends cooling-off rules, requires firms with more than three registered lobbyists to publicly list former members and senior staff they hire, and raises disclosure penalties to $500,000. These firms profit by hiring ex-lawmakers to sell access to their former colleagues, so the bill's restrictions cut directly at that business model.

industries.industry: Former members of Congress and senior congressional staff
industries.note: A lifetime ban on members and a six-year ban on senior staff would close the well-worn path from congressional office to six-figure lobbying work. This is a concentrated class whose private gain from the current system comes at the public's expense.
By lengthening the revolving door and increasing disclosure, the bill makes it costlier to retain recently departed lawmakers and staff as advocates, raising the price of influence over legislation.
